intro: Buddhist texts do not live only in books. They are copied by hand as devotion, chanted at funerals, built into sand mandalas and carved into stupas. They shape mindfulness programs in American hospitals and schools, and they are recited every week in temples across Chicago and its suburbs.

The first chapter of this unit follows the texts into art, ritual and American life, and asks what respectful engagement looks like, including debates over Buddha images as decor and over mindfulness taken out of its setting. The second chapter is your capstone. You will choose one passage, establish its text, set its context, gather three readings and build your own argument.

By the end you will be able to describe how Buddhist communities use their texts in practice, discuss debates about borrowing and respect fairly, and present a clear, cited, attributed argument about what one passage has meant to its readers and why.
bigQuestion: How do Buddhist texts live in the world today, and how can a student interpret one of them fairly and well?

test.q: About how many characters does the Chinese Heart Sutra have?
What happens to a sand mandala at the end?
choices: It is swept away and poured into water
It is buried in a stupa

test.q: What does 'aniconic' mean in early Buddhist art?
choices: Using symbols instead of a figure
test.why: Early carvings often show an empty seat or tree.

test.q: Why do many Buddhists object to Buddha images as casual decor?
choices: Images are honored like a revered teacher
Images are illegal in the U.S.
test.why: Consecrated images are treated with devotion.

test.q: When was the Buddhist Temple of Chicago founded?
test.why: Rev. Gyomay Kubose founded it in 1944.

test.q: What should a student do on a temple visit in this course?
test.why: The course describes practice and never leads it.

test.q: What does establishing the text include?
test.why: It identifies exactly what is read.

test.q: Which three readers does the capstone gather?
choices: A classical commentator, a modern teacher and a scholar
test.why: Three kinds of readers show different questions.

test.q: How does the Dhammapada commentary gloss dhamma in verse 1?
test.why: The commentary reads dhamma as mental states.

test.q: What should a capstone thesis argue?
choices: What the passage means to its readers and why they differ

test.q: When may a capstone quote a translation word for word?
choices: When it is a named public-domain translation
test.why: Other translations are paraphrased and marked.

write.prompt: Your capstone: choose one passage from this course. Establish its text and translation, set its context and school, summarize three readings (commentator, modern teacher, scholar), and argue what the passage means to its readers and why they differ. Cite every passage with text, section and translation.
tips: Quote exactly only from Muller (1881), Rhys Davids (1881) or the Cowell Jataka; paraphrase the rest and mark it.
Attribute every belief and reading; never write 'we' for a tradition.
Describe practices and sacred images with respect; never lead a practice.
Make a thesis someone could argue with, and answer from the texts.
